subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: I am Gurleen, and I keep going back to the birthday party. My friend Sangeeta sat down on the kitchen floor, pale and swaying, saying the room was spinning. I looked around to see if anyone else thought it was serious. Rohit was laughing at his phone. Two girls were arguing about music. Nobody looked worried, so I told myself Sangeeta was just being dramatic. I stood there with my hands in my pockets. Then Rohit's mother came in for the cake, took one look, sat down beside Sangeeta and phoned Sangeeta's family. I felt my face burn. I had looked at calm faces and decided calm meant fine.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta say was happening in the kitchen?
qa.a: Sangeeta said the room was spinning.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen decide that Sangeeta was just being dramatic?
qa.a: Gurleen looked around for cues and saw calm faces, so assumed it could not be serious; uncertainty was quietly settled by what the crowd showed.

qa.q: What could Gurleen have done when Sangeeta sat down on the floor?
qa.a: Gurleen could have stayed beside Sangeeta and asked directly "are you okay?", then fetched an adult such as Rohit's mother without waiting for anyone else to react.

qa.q: What might Rohit's mother have seen that Gurleen missed?
qa.a: Rohit's mother looked only at Sangeeta, not at the crowd's faces, and saw a pale, swaying child who needed care and an adult's call to Sangeeta's family.

grounding: A teenager sees a friend in trouble at a gathering, checks the calm faces around and decides it must be fine.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Teacher's note. On Wednesday I found Lokesh at the edge of a crowd in the east corridor where two boys were shoving each other. About fifteen students stood around, and nobody had called for a teacher. Lokesh told me later, "I looked at everyone else. They were just standing there, so I thought it must be a normal argument." I walked Lokesh to the office and thanked Lokesh for telling me plainly, and said checking with a teacher is never wrong. The head spoke with both boys the same day. — Rajni

qa.q: About how many students stood around the two boys?
qa.a: About fifteen students stood around the two boys.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh think it must be a normal argument?
qa.a: Lokesh looked around, saw everyone standing calmly, and took that as proof it was not serious; the uncertainty was answered by other people's calm.

qa.q: What turning point in Rajni's response could help Lokesh next time?
qa.a: Rajni thanked Lokesh for being honest and said checking with a teacher is never wrong, which gives Lokesh permission to act on a doubt.

qa.q: How might the two boys who were shoving have experienced fifteen students standing by?
qa.a: They may have felt the crowd was watching and expecting more, or may have felt trapped by the audience; nobody's calm face told them to stop.

grounding: A teenager sees a fight in a group, looks around to check whether it is serious and, seeing calm faces, decides it must be fine.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
School counsellor's note, Thursday.
Farida came to see me after lunch, upset. Yesterday at the bus stop, two older boys were shoving Sumit, a Class 9 student, against the railing. A group of about eight was watching.
Farida said she looked around at everyone's faces. They were calm, some even smiling. “So I thought it must be a joke between them,” she said. “Nobody else seemed worried.” Today she heard Sumit has a bruised shoulder and hasn't come to school.
I told her that freezing is common and that coming to me now was the right thing. I informed the vice-principal and called Sumit's parents this afternoon. We will talk to the students involved tomorrow.

qa.q: How many students were watching at the bus stop?
qa.a: About eight were watching.

qa.q: Why did Farida decide the shoving must be a joke?
qa.a: She felt unsure, and seeing calm and smiling faces made her think nobody was worried, so it must be fine.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do next, and why was it right?
qa.a: The counsellor reassured Farida, informed the vice-principal and called Sumit's parents the same afternoon, so Sumit gets support quickly.

qa.q: How might Sumit have felt as eight students just watched?
qa.a: Sumit probably felt scared and alone, seeing nobody step in during the shoving.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenager who saw a fight, read others' calm faces, and decided it must be fine.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
Saturday, 11:30 pm
Riya's birthday party. Someone brought a bottle and hid it in the terrace water tank room. Divyansh drank way too much. By nine he was slumped against the wall, eyes half closed, mumbling.
I looked around. Everyone was laughing, dancing, taking videos. Nobody looked scared. So I thought, okay, he's just being dramatic, it's fine. I even laughed.
At ten, Riya's mother came up, took one look and her face went white. She turned the music off, put him on his side, called his parents and a doctor friend. His father came in ten minutes.
I keep thinking: I saw him first. I looked at everyone's calm faces and decided nothing was wrong. Why did I trust their faces more than my own eyes?

qa.q: Where was the bottle hidden?
qa.a: It was hidden in the terrace water tank room.

qa.q: How does the diary writer feel now about the party?
qa.a: The writer feels guilty and shaken, realising that calm faces were trusted over what was clearly wrong.

qa.q: What did Riya's mother do, and what could the writer do next time?
qa.a: She stopped the music, put Divyansh on his side and called his parents and a doctor friend; next time the writer could fetch an adult straight away.

qa.q: How might Divyansh's father have felt arriving at the party?
qa.a: He was probably frightened and upset, rushing over after the call about his son.

grounding: A teenager writes about seeing a drunk friend at a party, reading everyone's calm faces and deciding it must be fine.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
The Dussehra fair in Rampur was all loudspeakers and jalebi smoke. Behind the bangle stall, Tanuja saw Pintu from the next lane slumped against a cart, eyes half open, a bottle by his foot. Three older boys stood nearby, laughing and sharing a packet of chips.
Tanuja slowed. Was he sick? Should she say something? The boys looked completely relaxed. Ganga, holding her hand, shrugged. "He's just being silly. Come, the ride's starting."
If it were serious, they'd look worried, Tanuja told herself, and let Ganga pull her to the giant wheel. At the top, she kept looking down at the cart.
When they got off, the chai-stall uncle was kneeling by Pintu, shouting for someone to fetch his father. Tanuja's stomach turned. She pushed forward. "Uncle, he's been like that since before the ride."

qa.q: Where did Tanuja see Pintu slumped?
qa.a: Against a cart behind the bangle stall.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja decide it must be fine?
qa.a: Tanuja felt unsure, and the older boys' relaxed laughter and Ganga's shrug made her doubt her own worry.

qa.q: What could Tanuja do next time she is unsure whether something is serious?
qa.a: Tell a nearby adult, like the chai-stall uncle, and let them check; being wrong costs very little.

qa.q: What would have changed for Pintu if Tanuja had spoken up before the ride?
qa.a: An adult could have reached Pintu sooner, instead of him lying alone by the cart while everyone else enjoyed the fair.

grounding: Shows a teenager who sees a drunk boy in trouble, checks the calm faces around her and decides it must be fine.
